name: Mosel

climate.koppen_name: Temperate, no dry season, warm summer

climate: Riesling and Müller-Thurgau sit in their sweet spot, so the wines can show the style they are known for.

sheet.place: The Mosel is a cool German river valley with steep slate slopes facing south. Riesling ripens slowly here. The wines come out light in alcohol, high in acid and balanced by a little sugar.
sheet.rules: German wine is graded by how ripe the grapes were, not how sweet the wine is. On the Mosel, Riesling needs at least 73 Oechsle for Kabinett, 80 for Spätlese and 88 for Auslese. Beerenauslese and Eiswein start at 110, Trockenbeerenauslese at 150.

claims.claim: The region is named after the Mosel river. It was called Mosel-Saar-Ruwer until 1 August 2007, then shortened to Mosel.

The PDO covers vines along the Mosel and its tributaries Saar and Ruwer. The river runs from Perl on the Luxembourg border to Koblenz. The spec splits it into Obermosel, Trierer Talweitung, Mittelmosel (Schweich to Moselkern) and the lower valley.

Wine law divides the region into Bereiche (districts). Wikipedia lists Burg Cochem, Bernkastel, Ruwertal, Saar, Obermosel and Moseltor. Bernkastel is the centre of the Mittelmosel. Saar and Ruwer are the two side valleys.
Graach (Himmelreich), Wehlen (Klosterberg, Sonnenuhr) and Zeltingen (Sonnenuhr) are neighbouring wine villages on the Mittelmosel, in the Bernkastel district.

Vines on the Mosel, Saar and Ruwer grow between about ⟦elev|210 and 1,230 feet|65 and 375 m⟧ above sea level, averaging about ⟦elev|590 feet|180 m⟧. About half the vineyards face south-east, south or south-west. The average aspect is 195 degrees, which is south-south-west.

Devonian rock dominates the region. From Mittelmosel downstream the river cuts a narrow valley into the Rhenish Slate Mountains. The Devonian rocks are mostly quartzitic sandstone, quartzite and clay slate. Limestone (Muschelkalk, Keuper) appears only on the Obermosel.
Slate soils warm quickly and drain well, and many top sites have little topsoil, only broken slate. Slate type varies by site and shapes the wine's mineral character.
Slate color varies from site to site. Blue and grey slate are common, and the VDP register uses 'blue and grey' for Himmelreich. A few sites, such as Ürzig, have red soils of sandstone and slate.

The steep slopes give the vines the most direct sunlight in the region. Average direct sun in the growing season is 652,000 Wh/m2, highest on steep and very steep sites. The river also reflects light onto the vines.

Bremmer Calmont on the lower Mosel, at about 65 degrees, is often called the steepest vineyard in Europe. The three sheet vineyards are less extreme. VDP slopes are 45 to 75 percent (Himmelreich) and 65 to 75 percent (Zeltinger Sonnenuhr).

The climate is cool. Average annual temperature is ⟦temp|49.5°F|9.7°C⟧ and the growing-season average is ⟦temp|57.4°F|14.1°C⟧. Rainfall averages ⟦rain|30 inches|760 mm⟧ a year, 60 percent of it in the growing season.

The sheltered river valley and the water moderate the climate, so it is mild for its latitude. Autumn nights bring fog as cold air from Hunsrück and Eifel meets warmer air over the river. The fog burns off by midday. Slow ripening and big day-night swings give fine fruit and a sharp, precise acidity.

Riesling is the main grape. It covered 59.7 percent of the region's vines in 2008 (⟦area|13,300 acres|5,390 ha⟧), well ahead of Müller-Thurgau at 14 percent. Total area then was about ⟦area|22,300 acres|9,034 ha⟧, the fifth largest of Germany's 13 regions.

Mosel Riesling is known for moderate alcohol, marked acidity and a balance of sweetness and acid. The spec says grapes reach only moderate sugar even at full ripeness, giving delicate wines with moderate alcohol. It describes Kabinett as having low to moderate alcohol and tense acid-sweet balance, and Spätlese and Auslese as usually made with some residual sugar. Typical aromas are pome fruit, stone fruit and citrus.
The steep slate slopes favour botrytis in ripe, humid autumns, which allows selection of Auslese, Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese.

Six Prädikat levels, set by must weight (ripeness at harvest, not final sweetness). Minimum for Mosel Riesling: Kabinett 73 Oechsle (9.5% vol potential), Spätlese 80 (10.6%), Auslese 88 (11.9%), Beerenauslese 110 (15.3%), Eiswein 110 (15.3%), Trockenbeerenauslese 150 (21.5%).

Eiswein grapes must be naturally frozen at harvest and pressing. Beerenauslese uses overripe, dried or botrytised berries. Trockenbeerenauslese uses more selection and shrivelled berries, giving the highest sweetness.
The Mosel Riesling minimums are higher than the older commonly quoted German figures of Kabinett 67-70, Spätlese 76 and Auslese 83. The Mosel PDO spec sets 73, 80 and 88 for Riesling.

Graacher Himmelreich is in the village of Graach, a VDP.GROSSE LAGE planted to Riesling. It faces south-west to south, lies at ⟦elev|360 to 1,070 feet|110 to 325 m⟧, and has a slope of 45 to 75 percent. Soil is blue and grey slate. Graded area is listed as ⟦area|163.09 acres|about 66 ha⟧.

Zeltinger Sonnenuhr is in Zeltingen. It is a VDP.GROSSE LAGE planted to Riesling, facing south-south-west to south, at ⟦elev|330 to 820 feet|100 to 250 m⟧, with a slope of 65 to 75 percent. Soil is stony, weathered grey Devonian slate. Graded area is ⟦area|51.25 acres|about 21 ha⟧.

Do not mix up the two Sonnenuhr sites. Wehlener Sonnenuhr is in Wehlen, graded at ⟦area|113.67 acres|about 46 ha⟧, grey-blue Devonian slate, ⟦elev|360 to 1,000 feet|110 to 320 m⟧. Zeltinger Sonnenuhr is its neighbor just downstream, in the next village, Zeltingen.

Wehlener Klosterberg is a slope in Wehlen, beside Markus Molitor's family house, Haus Klosterberg, which sits at the top. An importer describes it as a large, classically oriented slope with iron-rich Devonian slate. No official size, slope or exact aspect was found.

terms: Qualitätswein
German quality wine from one of the specified regions. It can be dry to sweet.
Prädikatswein
Germany's top tier, graded by how ripe the grapes are at harvest. Unless the label says dry or off-dry, expect some sweetness.
Kabinett
Light wine from fully ripe grapes of the main harvest, often semi-sweet with crisp acidity.
Spätlese
Late harvest. Often sweeter and fruitier than Kabinett.
Auslese
Select harvest from fully ripe or noble-rotted grapes.
Beerenauslese (BA)
Overripe berries picked one by one, often with noble rot. Rich, sweet dessert wine.
Trockenbeerenauslese (TBA)
Overripe berries shriveled on the vine, often with noble rot. Extremely rich and sweet. Trocken here means dried grapes, not a dry wine.
Eiswein
Ice wine, from grapes frozen naturally on the vine. The must is at least as sweet as a Beerenauslese.
Trocken, Halbtrocken
Dry and medium dry. Under EU rules a dry wine has no more than 4 g of sugar a liter, or a little more when its acidity is high. Medium dry has more sugar than that.
VDP, Grosses Gewächs (GG)
The VDP is an association of about 200 estates with rules stricter than the law. GG is its top dry wine from its best sites.
keyfacts: Mosel covers the valleys of the Mosel, Saar and Ruwer rivers, and before 1 August 2007 it was called Mosel-Saar-Ruwer.
Steep slopes and Devonian slate soils shape the wines, and the slate slopes store the day's heat.
The region has six districts (Bereiche), 19 Großlagen and 524 Einzellagen.

notes: Mosel Riesling is often light, low in alcohol, crisp and high in acidity, with flowery as well as fruity aromas.
High acidity and clearly defined flavors mark all Mosel wines, and some sweetness often balances the acid.
Saar and Ruwer wines can be just 6 to 9% alcohol, with intense fruit and high acidity.
The Mosel is also known for Eiswein, joining high acidity to concentrated sweetness.

blurb.text: A region along the Mosel, Saar and Ruwer rivers known for steep vineyard slopes above the water, including Bremmer Calmont, often called Europe's steepest vineyard. Riesling is its main grape, at 61% of vines. Northerly Rieslings are often light, lower in alcohol, crisp and high in acidity.
